item.title: ‘Beauty particle’ decay opens the door to the zeptoverse
item.description: A detector in the LHCb experiment CERN Welcome to the zeptoverse , the world of the unprecedentedly small. A new analysis of data from the Large Hadron Collider has uncovered an extraordinarily rare particle decay that opens the door to this realm and its secrets. The standard model of particle physics tabulates all known particles and how they interact, but it cannot explain dark matter and dark energy, which fill most of our universe. Consequently, researchers test its predictions in particle collider experiments, searching for signs of new particles and forces. Read more We’re solving the fundamental mystery of how reality is glued together Now, Paula Collins and her colleagues at the Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) experiment at CERN in Switzerland have found the first evidence of a rare decay involving the “beauty quark” particle, which opens a whole new world for these searches. Advertisement “People have been searching for it for more than 40 years,” she says. “Everyone’s just over the moon.” Beauty particles are often produced in the LHC’s particle smashes, but the researchers focused on a specific process where a beauty quark gets annihilated by an antiquark – its antimatter cousin – and their annihilation produces another particle and antiparticle pair, the electron-like muon and antimuon, which can be detected. This process is exceedingly rare and has eluded experiments for decades. Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter “These very, very rare decays, they’re almost impossible according to the current laws of physics,” says team member Harry Cliff at the University of Cambridge. “This happens only for one in 10 billion beauty particles.” The finding is still preliminary, with relatively large uncertainties and a significance level of 3.2 sigma, while the gold standard for a discovery is 5 sigma. This means the chance that the signal in the experiment occurred randomly instead of being meaningful is about 0.3 per cent. Cliff says future experiments ought to lower this uncertainty, but the data already reveals that we have reached the zeptoverse, a world at scales as small as sextillionths of a metre – the smallest ever explored. Yet undiscovered denizens of this world could influence the beauty particle decay process and because the process is so rare, researchers would immediately spot that change, says Collins. In this way, measuring this process is like surveying the zeptoverse. Read more Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics “It was really a surprise that the team would be able to see this very rare event,” says Jure Zupan at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. He says this was made possible by technical upgrades that the LHCb team has made in recent years. “It’s like a very powerful microscope where now you’re able to see much shorter distances because you don’t have a fog in front of your eyes,” says Zupan. “It’s absolutely exciting,” says Zoltan Lig

item.content:encoded: A detector in the LHCb experiment CERN Welcome to the zeptoverse , the world of the unprecedentedly small. A new analysis of data from the Large Hadron Collider has uncovered an extraordinarily rare particle decay that opens the door to this realm and its secrets. The standard model of particle physics tabulates all known particles and how they interact, but it cannot explain dark matter and dark energy, which fill most of our universe. Consequently, researchers test its predictions in particle collider experiments, searching for signs of new particles and forces. Read more We’re solving the fundamental mystery of how reality is glued together Now, Paula Collins and her colleagues at the Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) experiment at CERN in Switzerland have found the first evidence of a rare decay involving the “beauty quark” particle, which opens a whole new world for these searches. Advertisement “People have been searching for it for more than 40 years,” she says. “Everyone’s just over the moon.” Beauty particles are often produced in the LHC’s particle smashes, but the researchers focused on a specific process where a beauty quark gets annihilated by an antiquark – its antimatter cousin – and their annihilation produces another particle and antiparticle pair, the electron-like muon and antimuon, which can be detected. This process is exceedingly rare and has eluded experiments for decades. Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter “These very, very rare decays, they’re almost impossible according to the current laws of physics,” says team member Harry Cliff at the University of Cambridge. “This happens only for one in 10 billion beauty particles.” The finding is still preliminary, with relatively large uncertainties and a significance level of 3.2 sigma, while the gold standard for a discovery is 5 sigma. This means the chance that the signal in the experiment occurred randomly instead of being meaningful is about 0.3 per cent. Cliff says future experiments ought to lower this uncertainty, but the data already reveals that we have reached the zeptoverse, a world at scales as small as sextillionths of a metre – the smallest ever explored. Yet undiscovered denizens of this world could influence the beauty particle decay process and because the process is so rare, researchers would immediately spot that change, says Collins. In this way, measuring this process is like surveying the zeptoverse. Read more Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics “It was really a surprise that the team would be able to see this very rare event,” says Jure Zupan at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. He says this was made possible by technical upgrades that the LHCb team has made in recent years. “It’s like a very powerful microscope where now you’re able to see much shorter distances because you don’t have a fog in front of your eyes,” says Zupan. “It’s absolutely exciting,” says Zoltan Ligeti at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. This process is not only ultra-rare but mathematical theories predict it very well so investigating it makes for a particularly important test of the standard model, says Cristina Lazzeroni at the University of Birmingham in the UK. The new measurement is consistent with the standard model, but Ligeti says this does not mean that all possible new particles have been ruled out. In his view, the new measurement implies that effects of such particles must be small but not necessarily negligible and LHCb could quantify this further going forward. “What they measured is very interesting, but I think even more interesting is the promise [of future experiments],” says Zupan. Cliff, however, is worried about the future of the team’s research because last year the UK government withdrew funding from a planned LHCb upgrade. “We are now really scrambling to figure out will we be able to continue doing this sort of research,” he says. Journal Reference: arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2611.00230

item.title: Antarctica’s permafrost is emitting worrying amounts of CO2
item.description: Carbon dioxide emissions from ice-free ground in one area of Antarctica have grown fivefold in just five years, suggesting there may be a significant source of emissions we haven’t accounted for
item.dc:creator: Syris Valentine

item.title: Students gather to explore Hawaii's glorious night sky | Space photo of the day for Nov. 4, 2026
item.description: null Over 1,400 students gathered in Hawaii to learn about astronomy as part of the annual Journey Through the Universe program. (Image credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/J. Pollard) Students gathered under the stars in Hawaii recently to explore the awesome nature of the night sky together. What is it? From Oct. 19 to Oct. 22, more than 1,400 students on the Big Island of Hawaii gathered for the Journey Through the Universe event to explore astronomy together. The Journey Through the Universe program is currently in its 23rd year. It was originally developed by the National Center for Earth and Space Science Education (NCESSE) and later introduced in Hawaii by the international Gemini Observatory, a program within the U.S. National Science Foundation's NOIRLab (National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory) that works with the Department of Education Hilo-Waiākea. The program aims to introduce students in the Hilo-Waiākea public school system to astronomy as well as the incredible science that happens across Hawaii. The students who participate range from preschoolers to seniors in high school, so the program introduces some students to astronomy and helps others explore possible careers in STEM fields. This year, the program brought in 19 volunteer educators from scientific institutions like Maunakea Observatories and supported hands-on activities and lessons that went from the classroom to under the Milky Way . Why is it incredible? This image shows a growing love for astronomy in progress. From the red glow of a skywatching night (red light doesn't interfere with our ability to see at night like white light does) to the scattered telescopes and students standing under the stars, this scene paints a larger picture. This is just one program, but in bringing together volunteers, educators, scientists and students, the program has created an incredible and enduring learning experience. Whether or not students walk away wanting to pursue a career in STEM, this incredible immersion in astronomy can help to foster a lifelong appreciation for science and nature. It's always a great idea to gather under the stars and explore together.

item.title: Australia’s social media ban faces high court challenge
item.description: Australian teenagers are still using social media apps Shutterstock/Tada Images Almost one year on from the start of Australia’s landmark social media ban, it is clear that the law has failed to stop most children from accessing the platforms. Meanwhile, teenagers are hoping to overturn the policy through a challenge at the nation’s highest court. “I’m bringing the High Court case because young Australians have a right to be in the digital town square,” says Noah Jones, a primary witness opposing the ban in the case, which started hearings on 3 November. “This is the world of technology and I’m entitled to see it all and not be shut out.” Read more The truth about social media and screen time’s impact on young people Jones was 15 when the ban came into effect , prohibiting under-16s from accessing social media sites, including Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok. He was a plaintiff in the case, but withdrew due to the risk of costs being awarded against his family. Advertisement Now, the constitutional challenge is being led by advocacy group the Digital Freedom Project, alongside Reddit, which – like other social media behemoths – fears that Australia’s social media ban will be replicated elsewhere around the world. The primary argument before the court this week has been that the ban limits the freedom of political communication for under-16s. In spite of this challenge and widespread concerns about implementing and enforcing a social media ban for children, numerous nations, including the UK , Indonesia, Malaysia, Brazil and a number of EU members, say they, too, will follow suit. Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter From the moment the policy was announced, many experts warned that it would be unworkable and could have negative outcomes , and that the real target of any policy should be the platforms, their algorithms and what they allow online. The biggest failure of the policy highlighted by researchers is that most children have been able to keep their profiles. One study by Courtney Barnes at the University of Newcastle in Australia and her colleagues, who surveyed more than 400 under-16s prior to the ban and then again three months after it, found that 85 per cent were still using prohibited platforms. Such research and similar findings from Australia’s eSafety commissioner forced the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, to announce in June a doubling of the fines for social media companies from AUS$49.5 million to AUS$99 million ($35 million to $69 million) if breaches were identified. He also introduced a raft of new powers for the eSafety commissioner to compel companies to provide information about what they were doing to get kids off their sites. item.dc:creator: James Woodford
item.content:encoded: Australian teenagers are still using social media apps Shutterstock/Tada Images Almost one year on from the start of Australia’s landmark social media ban, it is clear that the law has failed to stop most children from accessing the platforms. Meanwhile, teenagers are hoping to overturn the policy through a challenge at the nation’s highest court. “I’m bringing the High Court case because young Australians have a right to be in the digital town square,” says Noah Jones, a primary witness opposing the ban in the case, which started hearings on 3 November. “This is the world of technology and I’m entitled to see it all and not be shut out.” Read more The truth about social media and screen time’s impact on young people Jones was 15 when the ban came into effect , prohibiting under-16s from accessing social media sites, including Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok. He was a plaintiff in the case, but withdrew due to the risk of costs being awarded against his family. Advertisement Now, the constitutional challenge is being led by advocacy group the Digital Freedom Project, alongside Reddit, which – like other social media behemoths – fears that Australia’s social media ban will be replicated elsewhere around the world. The primary argument before the court this week has been that the ban limits the freedom of political communication for under-16s. In spite of this challenge and widespread concerns about implementing and enforcing a social media ban for children, numerous nations, including the UK , Indonesia, Malaysia, Brazil and a number of EU members, say they, too, will follow suit. Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter From the moment the policy was announced, many experts warned that it would be unworkable and could have negative outcomes , and that the real target of any policy should be the platforms, their algorithms and what they allow online. The biggest failure of the policy highlighted by researchers is that most children have been able to keep their profiles. One study by Courtney Barnes at the University of Newcastle in Australia and her colleagues, who surveyed more than 400 under-16s prior to the ban and then again three months after it, found that 85 per cent were still using prohibited platforms. Such research and similar findings from Australia’s eSafety commissioner forced the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, to announce in June a doubling of the fines for social media companies from AUS$49.5 million to AUS$99 million ($35 million to $69 million) if breaches were identified. He also introduced a raft of new powers for the eSafety commissioner to compel companies to provide information about what they were doing to get kids off their sites. At that time, Albanese said countries around the world were following Australia’s lead on social media reform, but that social media companies weren’t doing enough to exclude children. Yet, nearly half a year later, and in spite of widespread evidence that the laws have had little effect on teens’ social media use, not a single fine has so far been issued. “Some kids hid accounts and devices from parents at first, but when accounts shut down, we all just made a new one or had someone older do the face scan,” says Jones. “Kids just laughed and kept using socials. Most kids I know have more social media accounts than last year because new platforms popped up and we tried them out.” Read more How AI poisoning is fighting bots that hoover data without permission Iain Corby at the Age Verification Providers Association in London says up to 80 per cent of children have kept their accounts, with half saying they were never challenged and over a third retaining access “thanks to the false ages they originally used to create the account”. “Australia has been a missed opportunity for those who hoped it would provide evidence on the benefits and drawbacks of age restrictions for social media, because the platforms did not implement the law in good faith,” says Corby. He says the UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has been much clearer about the requirement for highly effective age assurance when the UK brings in its restrictions next spring, and that ministers are “alive to the need for robust legislation that pre-empts loopholes”. “The social media platforms may think they have muddied the waters and avoided a successful precedent being set by Australia, but it is clear that lessons are also being learned by observers.” Susan McLean at CyberSafety Solutions, an Australian consultancy, says it is sad that teens around the world can access Instagram teen accounts with inbuilt safety settings, limited content and algorithmic controls, yet Australian children cannot because of the ban. She says this is pushing them to far less safe platforms. “I would never have found primary kids even knowing what Reddit was before the ban, but now it’s mainstream for kids as their vetting is easily bypassed,” says McLean. Read more Social media is dead – here’s what comes next Catherine Page Jeffery at the University of Sydney says her children have been able to retain their social media accounts and a “tentative conclusion” can be drawn that not that much has changed for Australian teens. She says there is no point doubling the penalty for social media firm breaches if the government isn’t going to enforce the law. “What does enforcement look like? Are we going to see that? Are we going to see these platforms being taken to court?” Jeffery asks. Lisa Given at RMIT University in Melbourne says governments around the world have been captivated by the headlines rather than the data. Instead of bans, efforts should instead be on online safety and digital duty of care, she says. It is impossible to keep children from interacting online and the focus of governments should be on making platforms safe, says Given. “My main message is that this isn’t the solution,” she says. “I think other countries really need to actually look at the data.” Noah Jones, the young witness in the High Court case, says the arguments made by the government’s lawyers in court this week left him dismayed. “I don’t matter as an Australian when they say I’m not an elector and they do not seem to know the shorthand of how people communicate today,” he says. “I resent when statements are made that I should form a local club to exchange ideas or drop pamphlets – that sounds like my mum’s childhood before the internet.”

item.title: A third of babies with peanut allergy grow out of it by 1 year old
item.description: Peanut allergies are common, but aren’t always lifelong Shutterstock/Aleksandr Grechanyuk More than a third of babies who were previously diagnosed with peanut allergies safely tolerated them during subsequent testing. This suggests that a surprisingly high proportion of infants’ peanut allergies last less than one year, allowing them to be freed from a lifetime of food restriction and worry. “Being able to identify those children early allows them to avoid an unnecessary allergy label and the burden of avoiding peanut,” says Tim Brettig at Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne. Read more The new drugs preventing allergic reactions to peanuts and other foods Since 2024, Australia has offered free treatment to all babies diagnosed with peanut allergy under the age of 12 months. The treatment, overseen by 10 public children’s hospitals across the country, involves feeding small but gradually increasing doses of peanut flour to allergic infants over two years to try to desensitise them, a strategy known as oral immunotherapy. Advertisement Before beginning the programme, babies are required to undergo an “oral food challenge” to confirm their allergy and assess its severity. It involves feeding them gradually escalating doses of peanut flour on a single day under medical supervision to see how much they can tolerate. The total given is 2500 milligrams, equivalent to two teaspoons of peanut butter. This is “above the threshold where we’d expect all children of this age to react if they have an allergy”, says Brettig, the medical lead of the programme. However, of the first 778 babies with previously diagnosed peanut allergy who undertook the oral food challenge, 35 per cent did not react to any dose of the peanut flour. This was despite the fact they had previously developed rashes, swelling, hives or other signs of allergic reactions after consuming peanut-containing foods, and had skin prick or blood test results consistent with a peanut allergy. “This was a surprising result for us – we expected a small proportion might pass the food challenge, but not 35 per cent,” says Brettig. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The parents of these babies were given the good news that their child was no longer considered to have a peanut allergy and didn’t need to begin the oral immunotherapy programme. They were also assured that they could safely reintroduce peanut into their child’s diet at home. The average time between the initial diagnosis of the peanut allergy and the oral food challenge was six months. It is unclear why a third of the infants stopped having reactions to peanut in this short window. “It might be that they had a transient allergy, where the immune system has an aberrant response to a food initially, but it doesn’t continue to occur,” says Brettig. item.content:encoded: Peanut allergies are common, but aren’t always lifelong Shutterstock/Aleksandr Grechanyuk More than a third of babies who were previously diagnosed with peanut allergies safely tolerated them during subsequent testing. This suggests that a surprisingly high proportion of infants’ peanut allergies last less than one year, allowing them to be freed from a lifetime of food restriction and worry. “Being able to identify those children early allows them to avoid an unnecessary allergy label and the burden of avoiding peanut,” says Tim Brettig at Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne. Read more The new drugs preventing allergic reactions to peanuts and other foods Since 2024, Australia has offered free treatment to all babies diagnosed with peanut allergy under the age of 12 months. The treatment, overseen by 10 public children’s hospitals across the country, involves feeding small but gradually increasing doses of peanut flour to allergic infants over two years to try to desensitise them, a strategy known as oral immunotherapy. Advertisement Before beginning the programme, babies are required to undergo an “oral food challenge” to confirm their allergy and assess its severity. It involves feeding them gradually escalating doses of peanut flour on a single day under medical supervision to see how much they can tolerate. The total given is 2500 milligrams, equivalent to two teaspoons of peanut butter. This is “above the threshold where we’d expect all children of this age to react if they have an allergy”, says Brettig, the medical lead of the programme. However, of the first 778 babies with previously diagnosed peanut allergy who undertook the oral food challenge, 35 per cent did not react to any dose of the peanut flour. This was despite the fact they had previously developed rashes, swelling, hives or other signs of allergic reactions after consuming peanut-containing foods, and had skin prick or blood test results consistent with a peanut allergy. “This was a surprising result for us – we expected a small proportion might pass the food challenge, but not 35 per cent,” says Brettig. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The parents of these babies were given the good news that their child was no longer considered to have a peanut allergy and didn’t need to begin the oral immunotherapy programme. They were also assured that they could safely reintroduce peanut into their child’s diet at home. The average time between the initial diagnosis of the peanut allergy and the oral food challenge was six months. It is unclear why a third of the infants stopped having reactions to peanut in this short window. “It might be that they had a transient allergy, where the immune system has an aberrant response to a food initially, but it doesn’t continue to occur,” says Brettig. Previous research has found that roughly a third of children with peanut allergies naturally grow out of them by age 6 , but this is the first time a high proportion of peanut allergies have been found to resolve on their own in infants. First week of life seems crucial for future allergy and eczema risk The mainstream view is that there are no particularly critical phases in the development of the immune system, but a study of hundreds of infants suggests otherwise The finding will “make a huge difference” to the children whose allergy labels were removed, says Brettig, because they won’t have to spend their lives being burdened by restricted food choices, anxiety about accidental exposure to peanut and the need to carry emergency medication. It may also prevent them from developing a true peanut allergy down the track, since peanut avoidance in early life is known to increase the risk of allergies later on , he says. The results also have wider implications for how peanut allergy is diagnosed and managed, says John Ziegler at the University of New South Wales, Sydney. Peanut allergy is commonly diagnosed based on clinical history and the results of skin prick or blood tests, usually without an oral food challenge. Routinely conducting oral food challenges would identify those who don’t need require treatment, and thus be cost-effective, says Ziegler. “The study confirms the importance of confirmation of the diagnosis of peanut allergy before embarking on oral immunotherapy,” he says. Due to the risk of severe reactions like anaphylaxis, such allergy treatments should only be conducted under medical supervision. Journal Reference: The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice DOI: 10.1016/j.jaip.2026.08.044

item.title: Hannah Fry: How to win The Traitors with maths (step one, don’t get made a traitor)
item.description: Hannah Fry in The Celebrity Traitors BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry In the late 1980s, in Soviet-era Russia, a young psychologist called Dmitry Davydov came up with a game about power and information. He called it Mafia and originally intended it as a teaching device, a way to demonstrate how a small, informed minority could manipulate the dynamics of a much larger, uninformed group and wield outsized power over those who were left floundering in uncertainty and paranoia. Almost 40 years later, that game has evolved into The Traitors – a TV show that is such a massive cultural phenomenon in the UK that the opening episode of this year’s celebrity edition drew more viewers to BBC One than watched England’s World Cup semi-final against Argentina. And recently I found myself in the middle of it. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column Sign up to newsletter In case you’ve been living under a rock, or just happen to have better things to do with your life than watch reality television (in which case, lucky you), the premise is simple. A small number of players, the traitors, secretly know who is on their side and get to “murder” someone each night. The remaining players, the faithful, are tasked with working out who the traitors are, voting to banish one suspect each evening. Inevitably, they spend most of their time rounding on innocent people and making them disintegrate. Which I strongly suspect might be at least half of what makes the whole thing so damn entertaining. Here’s the thing. When I got the call asking if I wanted to be on the show, of course I jumped at the chance. A game of incomplete information? That’s a mathematician’s dream, I thought. What a fun, stress-free way to try out some of my theories. On reflection, past me was an idiot. But we’ll come to that. Read more The surprising science that reveals what it takes to win The Traitors The challenge, as I saw it, was to find a way to cut through the uncertainty. All I had to do was monitor the evidence as the game unfolded, use the patterns in people’s behaviour to identify the traitors and then just persuade everyone else to vote them out. Bish bash bosh, victory. I started by combing through every previous series of the UK show, turning the joyful, chaotic mess of the series into a clean, delicious spreadsheet, determined to use all the statistical tricks I had at my disposal. Who voted for whom? Who travelled in cars together? Were there subtle statistical differences in the way traitors and faithful behaved that might give the game away? It turned out there were. They don’t necessarily want to send down an innocent person, nor do they want to persuade others into joining a stampede, drawing attention to themselves in the process. item.content:encoded: Hannah Fry in The Celebrity Traitors BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry In the late 1980s, in Soviet-era Russia, a young psychologist called Dmitry Davydov came up with a game about power and information. He called it Mafia and originally intended it as a teaching device, a way to demonstrate how a small, informed minority could manipulate the dynamics of a much larger, uninformed group and wield outsized power over those who were left floundering in uncertainty and paranoia. Almost 40 years later, that game has evolved into The Traitors – a TV show that is such a massive cultural phenomenon in the UK that the opening episode of this year’s celebrity edition drew more viewers to BBC One than watched England’s World Cup semi-final against Argentina. And recently I found myself in the middle of it. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column Sign up to newsletter In case you’ve been living under a rock, or just happen to have better things to do with your life than watch reality television (in which case, lucky you), the premise is simple. A small number of players, the traitors, secretly know who is on their side and get to “murder” someone each night. The remaining players, the faithful, are tasked with working out who the traitors are, voting to banish one suspect each evening. Inevitably, they spend most of their time rounding on innocent people and making them disintegrate. Which I strongly suspect might be at least half of what makes the whole thing so damn entertaining. Here’s the thing. When I got the call asking if I wanted to be on the show, of course I jumped at the chance. A game of incomplete information? That’s a mathematician’s dream, I thought. What a fun, stress-free way to try out some of my theories. On reflection, past me was an idiot. But we’ll come to that. Read more The surprising science that reveals what it takes to win The Traitors The challenge, as I saw it, was to find a way to cut through the uncertainty. All I had to do was monitor the evidence as the game unfolded, use the patterns in people’s behaviour to identify the traitors and then just persuade everyone else to vote them out. Bish bash bosh, victory. I started by combing through every previous series of the UK show, turning the joyful, chaotic mess of the series into a clean, delicious spreadsheet, determined to use all the statistical tricks I had at my disposal. Who voted for whom? Who travelled in cars together? Were there subtle statistical differences in the way traitors and faithful behaved that might give the game away? It turned out there were. For example, I discovered that traitors often make what I came to think of as “burn votes”. They don’t necessarily want to send down an innocent person, nor do they want to persuade others into joining a stampede, drawing attention to themselves in the process. So, instead, they throw their vote away on someone nobody else is voting for. They will also vote to banish their fellow traitors, but only when the writing is already on the wall. Someone who suddenly joins the vote against a traitor on the night they are finally banished, having never voted for them before, was a signal worth keeping an eye on. There were clues pointing in the other direction, too: failing to vote for a traitor on the night they are banished turned out to be a good signal that someone is faithful. And then there was a particularly ingenious observation made by viewers online: the producers often send the players who were shortlisted for murder into breakfast last. Occasionally, they throw one traitor into that group to keep everyone guessing, but never two. Which means that if someone arrived late to breakfast alongside a player who was subsequently revealed to be a traitor, that was a potentially useful clue that they were faithful. From left: Joanne McNally, Maya Jama, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry at breakfast in The Celebrity Traitors BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry As far as I could tell, there were no surefire ways to identify someone as a traitor (although Richard E. Grant would later do a spectacular job of proving me wrong). The faithful are so gloriously unpredictable (ahem. Joanne McNally) that anything suspicious could almost as easily have been done by a perfectly innocent player. But even so, buried in the noise, there were some small signals that could accumulate over time. Fortunately, there is a neat mathematical way to combine lots of weak evidence together – and it just so happens to have been used by Alan Turing to help crack the enigma code in the second world war. So, inspired by Turing, with a little help from our mutual, close personal friend Thomas Bayes, I set about building a Bayesian model that I could bring with me into the castle. It’s actually pretty simple: a points system that lets you update the odds of someone being a traitor as you go. The scores came from what had happened in previous series, and are almost entirely based on people’s voting patterns. +0.47 for a burn vote. -0.83 if you fail to vote for a traitor on the night they go down. For the nerdier among you, the units I was using are nats – a measure of how strongly the accumulated evidence favours one hypothesis over another – but you can just think of them as traitor points. I was as confident as I could be that, at the very least, the famous words of statistician George E. P. Box would prove true: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” Read more Hannah Fry: How OpenAI has caused an existential crisis in mathematics Unfortunately, there was one rather significant problem with my plan. Within about 15 minutes of arriving in the castle, they made me a traitor. (Technically I could have refused, but it happened in such a way that it would have meant my immediate downfall.) I went back to my room and sobbed into my spreadsheets. Still, I’m not about to let the small matter of being made a traitor (and catastrophically failing to be deceitful on national television ) get in the way of a good mathematical experiment. So, now that the final has aired and I know the way that the votes fell, I can finally run the numbers to see how the model would have played out in real time. And I’m delighted to say that the maths worked. Brilliantly, in fact. At every single round table, the maths has a traitor as top, or joint top. Not every innocent player escaped suspicion, and the model certainly wasn’t infallible. But there really are signals buried in that noise, and you really can use mathematics to detect them. (And yes, the irony that literally being buried is what got me into this mess is not lost on me). The trouble is, a mathematical model has one enormous advantage over a contestant on The Traitors . It doesn’t have to convince anyone to trust it. It doesn’t have to worry about being murdered or defend itself against accusations over breakfast, while trying to remember what normal facial expressions look like. And so even if I’d been a faithful, I suspect there was never any realistic chance of putting the mathematics to use within the game itself. Because, as Mafia was designed to demonstrate, the real power in a game like this isn’t just knowing the truth, it’s being able to shape what everyone else believes. And so, George, it turns out some models are right. It’s just that, sometimes, that’s the least of your problems. Hannah Fry: I lost my dad to Alzheimer’s. New research into its origins is amazing My lovely father died of Alzheimer’s last year, and since then, I’ve been digging into the disease to try to understand what happened to him. I was astonished to discover that scientists think it may start in the nose, says New Scientist’s new columnist, Professor Hannah Fry

item.title: Drone warfare in space: Swarms of autonomous, laser-shooting cubesats could defend Western satellites in orbit
item.description:
Mark is an award-winning freelance aviation and space journalist and author of the non-fiction book "N-4 DOWN: The Hunt for the Arctic airship Italia." He began writing for Space.com in 2026 and writes for a range of publications, from BBC Future to The Smithsonian’s Air and Space Quarterly and others. Mark won awards two years in a row at the Aerospace Media Awards for features he had written on the history of drones and astronaut training. Space grabbed hold of Mark’s imagination when, as a child, he saw the opening scene of "Star Wars: A New Hope" for the first time and has never let go. Away from the final frontier, Mark can be found walking his dog along the country lanes of England’s Cotswolds.

In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry. Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites . In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite. Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats . Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites , and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare . Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them. "We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space. item.content:encoded:
Mark is an award-winning freelance aviation and space journalist and author of the non-fiction book "N-4 DOWN: The Hunt for the Arctic airship Italia." He began writing for Space.com in 2026 and writes for a range of publications, from BBC Future to The Smithsonian’s Air and Space Quarterly and others. Mark won awards two years in a row at the Aerospace Media Awards for features he had written on the history of drones and astronaut training. Space grabbed hold of Mark’s imagination when, as a child, he saw the opening scene of "Star Wars: A New Hope" for the first time and has never let go. Away from the final frontier, Mark can be found walking his dog along the country lanes of England’s Cotswolds.

In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry. Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites . In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite. Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats . Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites , and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare . Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them. "We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space. Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities. In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) with two very small spacecraft. This effort, named Project Broadsword, will launch on SpaceX 's Transporter-21 rideshare mission. It will send up an 8U cubesat and a smaller 3U target craft, which Shield Space plans to maneuver from 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart to within 100 meters (330 feet) of each other and, through four stages of autonomy, from human-in-the-loop to "approximately" fully autonomous. (A cubesat unit, or U, is a cube that measures 10 cm, or about 4 inches, on a side.) Russia's Luch-2 satellite approaches another geostationary satellite on April 12, 2024, as tracked by the French company Aldoria's observation stations. (Image credit: Aldoria) The gaps between a true satellite-defense capability and this demonstration appear to be great, in terms of the technological and practical challenges of squeezing propulsion and power systems, AI compute power , sensors, the lasers the swarm needs to communicate and weapon systems onto small, lightweight maneuvering satellites. But it is a gap that Shield Space believes it can bridge through the purchase of relatively cheap off-the-shelf technology rather than more expensive bespoke designs. "Yes, it's a problem because of size, weight and power," Ritchie told Space.com. "We've had to totally innovate from scratch some elements of the mission… but we have only got roughly 100 cm by 100 cm [40 by 40 inches], so saving space or having systems that are already completely integrated is the main aim." "We have commissioned EnduroSat to build us an autonomous 8U cubesat that has chemical propulsion and its own imagery-collecting capability, which we will put our software on," said Dan Molland, co-founder and CTO of Shield Space, "and which we will then use to conduct our RPO . "The good thing about cubesats is they're very standardized and they're very off the shelf," he added. "There's always some level of adjusting you've got to do, but these cubesats are a lot more plug and play than more conventional platforms, which are usually all custom-built." Illustration of two Shield Space cubesats in orbit. (Image credit: Shield Space) Yet to focus on the technical issues may be to miss the point. "It takes an extraordinary amount of data to train the models and algorithms to achieve a fully autonomous mission," said Ritchie, "and the problem [unlike in the Ukraine war] is that data is not readily available. "We can train AI using synthetic data, but it's just not quite good enough for space. It's incredibly important to gather data from missions like this if we really want autonomous missions in the future." There is also the complexity of the AI needed in a war-fighting system. "Starling is a really great example," Molland told Space.com. "With Starling, you're essentially just asking a guidance system to make sure you stay within a given range of this or that satellite… But if you are controlling a swarm to deliver [a] military mission, you have a much more complex set of questions." It also comes with the challenge of ensuring that AI complies with any rules of engagement. But Ritchie and Molland believe these technical challenges can be overcome, and they have an aggressive schedule of demonstrations planned that they think will prove it. Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. and author of the book "War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics" (Edinburgh University Press, 2020), is more cautious about Shield Space's plans for the evolution of space warfare. "They remind me of a late Cold War missile-defense scheme called Brilliant Pebbles," he told Space.com. "It was one of the more advanced research and development programs in the Strategic Defense Initiative." The plan was to defend the U.S. against Soviet intercontinental ballistic missiles ( ICBMs ) by using thousands of small autonomous orbiting interceptors to destroy them by collision. "With enough investment, a lot is feasible," Bowen said. "But you're looking at many years of development and testing, solving the problem of testing kinetic weapons in space without leaving debris, and finding someone to buy the system." It is clear from Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine that the future of warfare includes swarms of low-cost autonomous drones — and Shield Space is already planning an aggressive schedule of missions to prove that this pattern applies to the final frontier as well. According to Ritchie, the startup hopes to quickly go from the first RPO demonstration to testing two full-sized 16U cubesats. It will then move on to a full carrier of 10 such cubesats, and then to a "super carrier" of 10 carriers, which will be deployed across multiple orbits. "We then get towards our future vision, which we call space-based carrier strike," said Ritchie. In this scenario, "responsive launch or pre-positioned carriers will give us an ability to protect and defend entire orbits, should you choose."

item.title: The Taurid meteor shower peaks tonight — and fireballs could steal the show
item.description: null Heads up stargazers! The Taurid meteor shower is upon us, bringing multiple peaks of activity that could see spectacular shooting stars and fireballs brighten November's sky. Here's where and when to look. What is the Taurid meteor shower(s)? Every autumn, Earth plows through streams of debris left behind by Comet Encke, a 3-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) ice body that orbits the sun once every 3.3 years. These debris streams produce two branches of the Taurid meteor shower : The Southern Taurids, active from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20 and the Northern Taurids, active from Oct. 20 to Dec. 10. As Earth plows through the debris streams, tiny particles slam into our atmosphere at 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), producing dazzling streaks of light across the night sky. Both branches of the Taurid meteor shower appear to travel away from a point of origin — or radiant — located in the constellation Taurus , which rises in the southeastern sky during November evenings. The Taurids are known for spawning brilliant fireball meteors, which can flare brighter than Venus as pebble-sized pieces of debris enter and burn up in the atmosphere. When to look for Taurid shooting stars The Southern Taurid shower features two distinct yearly peaks, the first of which occurred on Oct. 14. The second takes place overnight on Nov. 4-5 and is associated with an increase in fireball activity, when up to five meteors per hour could be seen blazing across the sky. The Northern Taurid stream, meanwhile, is expected to peak overnight on Nov. 11-12 with the same predicted hourly rate of up to five meteors per hour streaking across the dark, near moonless sky. How to spot Taurid meteors Head out to a dark sky location around midnight on the night of the peaks, when the shower's radiant in the constellation Taurus is positioned high in the southeastern sky, maximizing the number of meteors that can be seen. Remember not to stare directly at the radiant. Meteors seen close to the constellation Taurus strike our planet almost head-on, and so will have the shortest trails. Instead, pick out a patch of sky a little distance away, where the shooting stars will be at their most eye-catching as they skim through Earth's atmosphere. These essential stargazing accessories can help make a meteor-hunting trip! (Image credit: Created in Canva by Daisy Dobrijevic) Never use a telescope or binoculars to hunt for meteors, you want to take in as much of the sky as possible, not limit your field of view! And be sure to wrap up warm and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to adapt to the dark — a vital and often overlooked step for anyone hoping to catch even the faintest of meteors. Check out our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography , along with our guide to capturing fast-moving meteors if you want to create a permanent memory of the next big shower. item.title: Time to wake up MetOp-SG-B1 weather satellite
item.description: Following a short period in storage after arriving at Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana, the MetOp Second Generation-B1 satellite has been transferred to a cleanroom and removed from its transport container. The team is now preparing to reactivate this ‘sleeping beauty, and begin the final checks and preparations ahead of its launch, planned towards the end of the year.
item.content:encoded: Following a short period in storage after arriving at Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana, the MetOp Second Generation-B1 satellite has been transferred to a cleanroom and removed from its transport container. The team is now preparing to reactivate this ‘sleeping beauty, and begin the final checks and preparations ahead of its launch, planned towards the end of the year.

item.title: Before the Dawn in America’s Heartland
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Before the Dawn in America’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 18, 2026 The predawn hours brought clear skies over much of the eastern United States on October 18, 2026. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station seized the opportunity to capture this wide-angle photo at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time (09:54 Universal Time), with illuminated cities large and small arrayed across the darkened landscape. The U.S. Midwest’s largest metropolitan areas , such as Chicago, Illinois, and Detroit, Michigan, stand out as some of the brightest features. Mid-sized cities—including Indianapolis, Indiana; Cincinnati, Ohio; and Louisville, Kentucky—and their interconnections along state and interstate highways also shine brightly. Above the web of nighttime lights and Earth’s lower atmosphere, a diffuse layer of green and orange is visible along the horizon to the left. This band of light is airglow , produced when sunlight strikes atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere and causes them to eject photons . To the right, light from the Sun arcs across the horizon; sunrise was about an hour away on the East Coast and about two hours away in Chicago. Astronaut photos and other remote sensing observations of nighttime lights are scientifically valuable for tracking changes in the built environment. For example, Chicago’s lightscape appears a homogeneous pale yellow in the wide view above. But in detailed photos, like the one below, a range of colors stemming from different types of lighting is discernible. Using NASA’s extensive Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth archive, researchers have developed a method for distinguishing lighting types within the pixels of nighttime photos. Systematically quantifying urban lights’ brightness, color, and extent can provide insight into how cities grow and evolve . March 1, 2024 Satellite sensors also observe changes to lighting. In particular, NASA’s Black Marble nighttime lights product suite uses satellite observations to produce science-quality records of nighttime lights across the globe at daily, monthly, and yearly time scales. In the eastern U.S., scientists have used these data to track everything from power outages and restoration following major storms to lighting changes associated with new infrastructure to transitions to LED lighting from older forms. Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-226709 was acquired on October 18, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters, and photograph ISS070-E-105097 was acquired on March 1, 2024, with a Nikon D5 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. They are provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The images were taken by members of the Expedition 75 and Expedition 70 crews, respectively. The images have been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth . Story by Lindsey Doermann. item.title: Feet-stiffening socks could help you run further for longer
item.description: The socks you wear while running could make a big difference to your personal best Artur Widak/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Introducing tight bands in socks around the ball of the foot seems to make walking and running easier. The effects of these socks, which stiffen the feet, are equivalent to the reduced energy expenditure that the average person would experience if they lost 2 kilograms, according to the researchers behind them. Owen Beck at the University of Texas at Austin says he hopes to see elite runners in the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics using these socks, which he developed with Hui Tang , also at the University of Texas at Austin. “Our back-of-the-envelope estimates suggest that wrapping the foot in the new socks could improve marathon performance by 1 to 2 minutes,” says Beck. Read more Why slow running could be even more beneficial than running fast Since diverging from chimpanzees around 6 million years ago, human feet have become much stiffer than those of other apes, which assisted our bipedalism. Beck and Tang first wondered if they could take this stiffness further by tweaking footwear. However, previous attempts to reduce walking and running effort using shoes with stiffer midsoles or inserts have failed, so then the pair turned to socks. Advertisement They are made of a common synthetic yarn blend, typical of athletic socks. Beck and Tang tightly knitted three 1-millimetre wide bands at a 30-millimetre-wide region around the ball of the foot. This results in 24 times more pressure being applied to feet compared with regular, control socks. To test them, they recruited 12 adults of both sexes who had no known health conditions. The researchers analysed how they walked while wearing the foot-stiffening socks, control socks and no socks. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter Participants then walked on a treadmill while wearing shoes with the stiffened socks and control ones for 5 minutes. Beck and Tang measured their VO2 max, the maximum amount of oxygen the body can absorb during high-intensity exercise. This allowed them to determine how much energy they burned in each of the walking experiments, known as metabolic expenditure. The foot-stiffening socks reduced this expenditure in 10 of 12 of the participants by 2 per cent more than the control socks. That is equivalent to the average person losing 2 kilograms, according to the researchers. This reduced expenditure probably doesn’t mean the socks lead to wearers getting fewer health benefits, such as weight loss, from walking or running compared with those wearing regular socks, says Beck. “Reducing the whole-body metabolic rate means we have better walking endurance, we sweat less during hot days and we can walk faster for the same effort [that we would use] using commercially available socks.” The socks work by enabling the ankle and its muscles to push off at a slower velocity, he says. item.content:encoded: The socks you wear while running could make a big difference to your personal best Artur Widak/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Introducing tight bands in socks around the ball of the foot seems to make walking and running easier. The effects of these socks, which stiffen the feet, are equivalent to the reduced energy expenditure that the average person would experience if they lost 2 kilograms, according to the researchers behind them. Owen Beck at the University of Texas at Austin says he hopes to see elite runners in the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics using these socks, which he developed with Hui Tang , also at the University of Texas at Austin. “Our back-of-the-envelope estimates suggest that wrapping the foot in the new socks could improve marathon performance by 1 to 2 minutes,” says Beck. Read more Why slow running could be even more beneficial than running fast Since diverging from chimpanzees around 6 million years ago, human feet have become much stiffer than those of other apes, which assisted our bipedalism. Beck and Tang first wondered if they could take this stiffness further by tweaking footwear. However, previous attempts to reduce walking and running effort using shoes with stiffer midsoles or inserts have failed, so then the pair turned to socks. Advertisement They are made of a common synthetic yarn blend, typical of athletic socks. Beck and Tang tightly knitted three 1-millimetre wide bands at a 30-millimetre-wide region around the ball of the foot. This results in 24 times more pressure being applied to feet compared with regular, control socks. To test them, they recruited 12 adults of both sexes who had no known health conditions. The researchers analysed how they walked while wearing the foot-stiffening socks, control socks and no socks. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter Participants then walked on a treadmill while wearing shoes with the stiffened socks and control ones for 5 minutes. Beck and Tang measured their VO2 max, the maximum amount of oxygen the body can absorb during high-intensity exercise. This allowed them to determine how much energy they burned in each of the walking experiments, known as metabolic expenditure. The foot-stiffening socks reduced this expenditure in 10 of 12 of the participants by 2 per cent more than the control socks. That is equivalent to the average person losing 2 kilograms, according to the researchers. This reduced expenditure probably doesn’t mean the socks lead to wearers getting fewer health benefits, such as weight loss, from walking or running compared with those wearing regular socks, says Beck. “Reducing the whole-body metabolic rate means we have better walking endurance, we sweat less during hot days and we can walk faster for the same effort [that we would use] using commercially available socks.” The socks work by enabling the ankle and its muscles to push off at a slower velocity, he says. This requires less activation and less metabolic energy, leading to more economical muscle contractions. Unlike a stiffened shoe, the socks allow the toes to flex and the arch to recoil more freely, he says. Want to move fast? Look for these materials in your next running shoes Spiked running shoes with a rubbery material between the inner and outer soles, and a stiff plate to improve stability, seem to help people move faster Thomas Püschel at the University of Oxford says the idea that a stiff foot makes walking less metabolically costly has been around for a long time, but nobody had managed to show it in people while they were walking until now. “The team’s clever insight was that those earlier attempts [with shoes] also stopped the foot moving when it needs to, right at the end of the step.” The applications of the socks are yet to be tested. But Beck says that, in theory, anyone whose feet have lost some of their shape, say through old age, could benefit. The researchers already have a sponsored research agreement with the shoe company New Balance to commercialise the socks, says Beck. However, Püschel warns that other explanations for the results cannot be ruled out, such as the volunteers changing how they walked when they knew they had the socks on. “It’s a promising first demonstration, rather than evidence that these socks will change anyone’s daily life,” he says. Journal reference: Royal Society Proceedings B DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2026.1467

item.title: NASA asks industry for ideas about saving Hubble Space Telescope
item.description: null NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency , was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009. The observatory's groundbreaking achievements include helping to show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating — a discovery that won the Nobel Prize — as well as a swath of finds about planets, galaxies, stars and other parts of the universe . Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers , NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September. Hubble is also widely appreciated by the public. People have long enjoyed and celebrated its iconic images , such as the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation," a gorgeous shot that has been revisited several times over the decades. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer. In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024 .) NASA declined , however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory. But things have changed, apparently. Isaacman, who in December 2025 became NASA administrator, said in an Oct. 30 agency statement that Hubble's science return means the agency should "be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible" — especially if doing so would be a cost savings compared with launching another mission. In an Oct. 30 post on X , Isaacman added that it's "still worth exploring the options" and noted that NASA had previously considered "a far lower-cost solution" to keep the observatory flying. "That was then. Still worth the effort — Hubble deserves it," he added. The new RFI also allows for alternative scenarios, however, which could include a "safe, controlled reentry into Earth's atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission." Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated. item.content:encoded: null NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers , NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer. In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024 .) NASA declined , however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory. But things have changed, apparently. Isaacman, who in December 2025 became NASA administrator, said in an Oct. 30 agency statement that Hubble's science return means the agency should "be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible" — especially if doing so would be a cost savings compared with launching another mission. In an Oct. 30 post on X , Isaacman added that it's "still worth exploring the options" and noted that NASA had previously considered "a far lower-cost solution" to keep the observatory flying. "That was then. Still worth the effort — Hubble deserves it," he added. The new RFI also allows for alternative scenarios, however, which could include a "safe, controlled reentry into Earth's atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission." Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated. Earlier this year, NASA worked with Katalyst Space Technologies on a $30 million mission that aimed to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which is also falling back to Earth due to orbital drag. That long-shot rescue mission — which was developed quickly to race against accelerated solar activity, which ballooned Earth's atmosphere and increased drag — launched successfully this summer. But control issues prevented Katalyst's LINK spacecraft from meeting up with Swift. Swift is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere tomorrow (Nov. 4) after 22 years of operations — far past its two-year design lifetime.

item.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
item.description: null New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes. Dense stellar environments do still exist in the modern universe at the hearts of galaxies; however, these aren't conducive to the types of collisions that would birth ultra-massive stars. That is because there are already supermassive black holes at the hearts of modern galaxies, and their immense gravitational influence speeds up orbiting stars, meaning collisions that do occur are high-speed and destructive, thus failing to birth overmassive stars. "Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster," team member Claire Williams, of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), said in a statement. "When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole." My, haven't you grown? How did supermassive black holes get so big so fast? The existence of supermassive black holes before the universe was even 1 billion years old is something that has puzzled astronomers since the JWST started spotting them in 2022. This is because black holes should need at least 1 billion years to complete the feeding and merger processes that result in a "supermassive" status of possessing millions or billions of times the mass of the sun. One suggestion put forward by scientists to explain this is that supermassive black holes don't start out from scratch. Instead, they form from black hole seeds called intermediate-mass black holes. An illustration shows a massive black hole seed next to a standard stellar mass black hole (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva)) Normally, when a massive star collapses, it births a stellar-mass black hole possessing a mass between 10 and 100 times the mass of the sun. This is considerably smaller than supermassive black holes that dominate the hearts of all modern galaxies with masses millions to billions of times the mass of our star. Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to sit between these two families of cosmic titans with masses between 100 and 100,000 times that of the sun.
